Context Text: The Healthcare Technology Self-Efficacy Scale was used to assess healthcare technology self-efficacy. Our group has revised the Chinese version, which can be used to assess the confidence of individuals when using health technology or receiving services provided by health technology. The scale contains 12 items and 3 dimensions: technology, service, and web. A 5-point Likert scale was used, ranging from 1 = "Strongly Disagree" to 5 = "Strongly Agree", with entries 3, 6, and 10 reverse-scored.
Notes: 396 community-dwelling patients aged 60-88 with coronary heart disease, four communities in Qingdao, China, paper questionnaires December 2023 - May 2024 (Zhao et al. 2025, PLOS ONE); Chinese versions of each instrument.

Context Text: The eHealth Literacy Scale (eHEALS) was used to evaluate eHealth literacy. The Chinese version of eHEALS includes 8 items and 3 dimensions: application ability, evaluation ability, and decision-making ability. Each item is scored on a five-point Likert scale from 1 ("strongly disagree") to 5 ("strongly agree").
Notes: 396 community-dwelling patients aged 60-88 with coronary heart disease, four communities in Qingdao, China, paper questionnaires December 2023 - May 2024 (Zhao et al. 2025, PLOS ONE); Chinese versions of each instrument.

Context Text: The Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS) which was compiled by Xiao in 1994, was used to measure social support. The scale includes 10 items and 3 dimensions: subjective support, objective support, and utilization of support. Items 1-4 & 8-10: Select one option per item (1-4 points). Item 5: A-D options (4-point scale: 1 = none to 4 = full support). Items 6-7: 0 points without sources; score = number of sources listed.
Notes: 396 community-dwelling patients aged 60-88 with coronary heart disease, four communities in Qingdao, China, paper questionnaires December 2023 - May 2024 (Zhao et al. 2025, PLOS ONE); Chinese versions of each instrument. Item 5 (a sum) not shipped; items 6-7 are counts of support sources.

Context Text: Attitudes towards communication were evaluated with the reduced version of the Attitudes Towards Communication questionnaire (ACO-R) of 12 items. This scale was Likert type with 5 response options, being 1 = strongly disagree and 5 = strongly agree. The higher the score, the higher the positive attitudes towards communication. The original instrument consisted of 25 items divided in 3 dimensions: affective (evaluated inversely), cognitive and behavioral.
Notes: 193 direct patient care nurses from four public hospitals in the Valencian Community, Spain, convenience sample (Giménez-Espert et al. 2026, PLOS ONE); Spanish-language questionnaire. No covariates deposited.

Construct Name: UNIPSICO job demands and resources scales + reduced CESQT burnout
Context Text: In this study, psychosocial risks were grouped into two categories: job demands and resources. The majority of the demands was examined with the UNIPSICO battery. All scales were Likert type with 5 response options, being 0 = never and 4 = very frequently: every day. The demands were interpersonal conflicts (6 items), inequity (6), role conflict (4), role clarity (5) and workload (6). The resources were social support (6), autonomy (5) and resources (8). Burnout was measured with a reduced version of the Burnout Syndrome Evaluation Questionnaire (CESQT) of 7 items (0 = never, 4 = very frequently: every day).
Notes: 193 direct patient care nurses from four public hospitals in the Valencian Community, Spain, convenience sample (Giménez-Espert et al. 2026, PLOS ONE); Spanish-language questionnaire. No covariates deposited. Scale order within the 53-item block is not recoverable, so the scales ship as one table.

Context Text: The violence demand was measured with an adaptation of a workplace violence questionnaire. It was Likert type with 5 response options, being 1 = strongly disagree and 5 = strongly agree. It consists of 6 items divided in 3 types of workplace violence: physical, verbal and psychological. All types of workplace violence were asked both from patients, patients' families or visitors and from colleagues, supervisors or managers.
Notes: 193 direct patient care nurses from four public hospitals in the Valencian Community, Spain, convenience sample (Giménez-Espert et al. 2026, PLOS ONE); Spanish-language questionnaire. No covariates deposited.

Construct Name: Multidimensional Negative Emotions Self-Regulatory Efficacy Scale (MNESRES), Spanish version
Context Text: Multidimensional Negative Emotions Self-Regulatory Efficacy Scale (MNESRES). Participants rated their capacity to manage different emotions on a scale of 1-5 (1 = not at all well; 5 = very well) using 3 items for each: anger/irritation (e.g., "How well can you avoid flying off the handle when you get angry?"), despondency/sadness, shame/embarrassment, fear and guilt. The formulation, selection and phrasing of the challenges presented in each item, carrying different degrees of difficulty, followed Bandura's guidelines.
Notes: 1,695 Spanish adults aged 20-94 born in Spain, mostly Madrid area, recruited through the Open University in Madrid (UDIMA) and students' relatives and friends, 2014-2017 (Caprara et al. 2020, PLOS ONE); Spanish versions administered individually. All 40 administered items ship; the paper's 15-item scale is identified in the dictionary notes.

Construct Name: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS), Spanish version
Context Text: Participants rated the degree to which they generally experience the ten negative emotional states in the Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS), on a scale of 1-5 (1 = not at all; 5 = very much). We used the Spanish version of this scale, and the emotions referred to as "distressed", "upset", "afraid", "scared", "nervous", "jittery", "hostile", "guilty", "irritable" and "ashamed" were the ten items included in this score.
Notes: 1,695 Spanish adults aged 20-94 born in Spain, mostly Madrid area, recruited through the Open University in Madrid (UDIMA) and students' relatives and friends, 2014-2017 (Caprara et al. 2020, PLOS ONE); Spanish versions administered individually.

Context Text: The 44-item Big Five Inventory answered 1-5 from 'disagree strongly' to 'agree strongly'. Shipped as one table: the five factors are subscales of one instrument on one response format, and the item code carries the factor letter (bfi_1_e, bfi_2_a, ...) for anyone who wants to split them.
Notes: 272 university students in Pakistan, private and public institutions (Batool & Khan 2024, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.13760224). Both instruments were administered in English in one sitting and share one id. RESPONSES ARE RAW AGREEMENT: the deposit stored its reverse-keyed items already flipped, which would have mixed two response directions in one table, so they were restored with 6-x and 5 always means 'agree strongly'. The deposit had also missed the BFI's sixteenth reverse-keyed item ('Is sometimes shy, inhibited'), which under this convention needed no handling. Item text is in the .sav's variable labels but is blocked by ruling: the BFI-44 is registered `block` and the GAAIS `hold`.

Context Text: Fifteen items answered 1-5 on accepting artificial intelligence, over the four canonical technology-acceptance constructs the item codes carry: perceived usefulness (pu1-3), perceived ease of use (peu1-4), attitude (att1-4) and behavioural intention (bi1-4). Notes: 702 pre-service mathematics teachers (Mersin 2025, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17631162). All four measures were answered in one survey and share one id, with NO missing data and no covariates at all -- the deposit ships the 29 item columns and nothing else. The four groupings are the deposit's own, from its description.
